cases.persona: A8 Robin and Kim (audit, invented)
cases.situation: Robin and Kim are buying a $1,600 sofa and split it evenly, so Robin pays $800. Robin has $1,000 spare in November. (Amounts in dollars; the audit used pounds.)
cases.why: Only Robin's share is judged: $1,000 - $800 = $200 left. The split itself is right (the audit agreed); whether $200 left needs a caution is decided by the safety-net rules once Household lands.

cases.persona: Jo and Sam (invented)
cases.situation: Jo has $1,000 spare in November. Jo's partner Sam has $5,000 in an account of their own, but has not agreed to share it with Decide. Jo is looking at a $2,000 purchase.
cases.why: Sam's money is not counted without Sam's opt-in, so Jo's $1,000 is all there is: not enough for $2,000. On 1 December, $1,000 left from November plus $1,000 spare in December covers it.

cases.persona: Ali and Noa (invented)

cases.why: $1,000 - $500 = $500 left, so it fits. Because the card is in both names, the answer states that each of them can be asked to pay all of it.

cases.persona: Max and Lee (invented)
cases.situation: Max and Lee split $2,000 rent evenly. Max's $1,200 of bills includes only his $1,000 half. Max has $1,000 spare in November and is looking at a $500 purchase.
cases.why: Only Max's share of the rent counts as his bill: $1,000 - $500 = $500 left. Counting the whole $2,000 rent would wrongly add $1,000 to his bills and leave nothing spare.

cases.persona: Eve and Dan (invented)
cases.situation: Eve paid Dan $300 this month to settle up their shared costs. That transfer is marked as settling up, not as spending. Eve has $1,000 spare in November and is looking at a $500 purchase.
cases.why: Settling up moves money between partners for costs already counted, so it is not new spending: $1,000 - $500 = $500 left. Counting the $300 as spending would count those costs twice.
